I like Dex, but his analogy here almost feels intentionally ignorant of the situation here.

"If public e-bike company gave you a subscription on rides and you proceeded to around ripping out batteries and sticking them in your own bike and ride around town, you’d get banned for that too. Especially if your bike was poorly wired and overloaded the batteries/cause them to flame up etc."

Let's fix the analogy.

First, we need to separate the "e-bike" and the "battery". The bikes are a commodity. You can download 10 options for free on GitHub. You just have to bring your own battery.

Now we have lots of bikes and a shortage of batteries. Only two companies make batteries. Well, there's actually like 10, but 8 of them are less reliable and only hold 1/4th the charge. One of them makes your bike drive off the road sometimes. So we're stuck with two real options.

The batteries are EXPENSIVE. Like $100 each. (assume they're single-use for this to work, again this is the bullshit Dex gave me to work with here). Some people only use $10 of charge a month. Others user $100 a week. We all pay roughly the same rate when we need new batteries.

Then suddenly, one of the two battery companies offers a new plan - $200/month, but you get up to $5,000 in battery replacements. HOORAH!

But there's a catch - you can only use the batteries in THEIR bikes. Wait, what? There's so many options! Sucks for you, they want you to use THEIR bikes. Btw, you can't actually modify them or fix them when they break. And they break. A LOT. Constantly even. And they hide all the details of how they're built.

Your friend next door has a bike from GitHub. It works great. He has no issues. The schematics are public. He can fix it however he want. He can even use Anthropic's batteries! He just has to pay full price.

You get a massive discount, you just have to deal with a shitty, opaque, unreliable, slow, fucked up bike.

recent_posts.title: Anthropic SpaceX compute deal explained and what it means for AI competition
recent_posts.summary: Anthropic struck a surprise compute deal with SpaceX/XAI, leasing roughly 300 megawatts (220,000 H100s) of Colossus 1 capacity — nearly the entire cluster — because Anthropic massively underestimated demand, seeing 80x annualized growth instead of the planned 10x. The deal explains recent Claude usage limit changes: they were compute rationing, not revenue grabs. The partnership is analyzed through a three-factor AI competition framework (research, data, compute): XAI has compute but lacks quality training data and researchers; Anthropic has research and data but lacked compute; Cursor has unique coding interaction data but no compute — making the XAI-Cursor deal and Anthropic-SpaceX deal logical complements. OpenAI is the only lab with all three. The analysis also covers API rate limit increases for enterprise tiers, speculation that Azure may be proxying Anthropic API calls rather than hosting models directly, and why Colossus 1 was largely idle (Grok has minimal inference demand). The broader takeaway is that compute lead times of 2+ years create structural advantages, and both deals are driven by mutual hatred of OpenAI more than affection between the parties.

recent_posts.title: GitHub alternatives compared from GitLab to Forgejo and next-gen options
recent_posts.summary: A deep-dive comparison of GitHub alternatives as developers consider leaving due to reliability issues. GitLab is criticized for poor UX and massive codebase complexity. Bitbucket is dismissed as primarily a cost-saving tool for Atlassian shops. Forgejo and Codeberg emerge as the recommended open-source self-hostable options, praised for clean Go codebase, solid release tooling, and nonprofit governance. Pierre's code.sto is highlighted as a next-generation Git infrastructure built for high-throughput agentic workflows. Graphite (acquired by Cursor) and Entire (founded by GitHub's ex-CEO) are flagged as potential Gen 3 players. The piece ends with a lament about the fragmentation of GitHub's developer community, arguing that no tool can replace the social graph that GitHub built over 20 years.

top_posts.title: From Twitch engineer to Y Combinator founder
top_posts.summary: A software engineer shares their journey from working at Twitch for 5 years to founding their own startup. The story covers their early career struggles, learning experiences at different teams within Twitch, the decision-making process behind quitting, failed attempts at other startups, and eventually building a creator tool called Round that led to acceptance into Y Combinator. Key themes include the importance of mentorship, talking to users, and recognizing when corporate environments no longer align with personal goals.

top_posts.title: Why xstate store might be the next big thing in state management
top_posts.summary: Introducing xstate store, a new state management tool that offers a modern, lightweight approach combining the best features from libraries like zustand and Redux toolkit. It excels in type inference, separation of context and transitions, and provides an upgrade path from simple stores to more complex state machines. xstate store is also framework-agnostic, which simplifies logic separation from the UI layer.

top_posts.title: Moving to a new browser: Zen
top_posts.summary: The author shares their frustrating experiences with the Arc browser due to its performance issues and lack of updates. They explore and evaluate various browsers such as Chrome, Brave, Edge, Vivaldi, and Zen. The author ultimately decides to switch to the open-source Zen browser, praising its customizability, user-focused development, and supportive community. They appreciate Zen's continuous improvement and responsiveness to user feedback, unlike the more established but less user-attentive browsers.

top_posts.title: GitHub fake star economy and its impact on VC funding decisions
top_posts.summary: A deep dive into the fake GitHub star economy, covering a peer-reviewed CMU/NC State/Socket study that identified ~6 million suspected fake stars across 18,600 repos. The investigation reveals a mature shadow market where stars sell for 3 cents to 90 cents each, with ROI of up to 117,000x when used to manufacture VC funding traction. Key findings include detection heuristics like fork-to-star and watcher-to-star ratios, analysis of specific AI and blockchain repos showing manipulation signals, how VC firms like Redpoint explicitly use star counts as sourcing benchmarks, and GitHub's reactive-only enforcement leaving the fake account infrastructure largely intact. The piece also covers legal exposure under FTC rules and SEC wire fraud precedents, and recommends alternative metrics like contributor activity and package downloads.

top_posts.title: Why Everyone Loves Zustand
top_posts.summary: Zustand is a state management library for React that simplifies state management with a small and efficient API. Unlike Redux, Zustand reduces boilerplate and offers a React hook-based solution. This post dives into using Zustand to refactor an application named Teemo, demonstrating how to instantiate and access state in a more straightforward manner. Zustand's advantages include its small package size, ease of setup, and ability to prevent unnecessary re-renders by selecting specific state slices. The post also briefly touches on the author's experiences with state management in a more complex app and comments on the use of context and middleware.
